base.prose:
- **Patients** benefit from continuity of care with their clinical history, identity, and entitlements following them across facilities and programmes rather than being reconstructed at each encounter.
- **Health workers** benefit from reduced administrative burden, fewer duplicate data entry tasks, and access to more complete and reliable information at the point of care.
- **Health programme managers** gain a consistent, cross-cutting data foundation that supports monitoring, evaluation, and resource planning across programmes rather than within silos — and, as data is aggregated across programmes and sectors, a basis for the intelligence that informs sector objectives, financing decisions, and operational guidelines.
- **Ministries of Health** gain visibility and governance over a coherent national digital health ecosystem rather than a patchwork of disconnected systems.
- **Ministries of Finance and cross-sector counterparts** benefit from the transparency and accountability that shared DPI-H makes possible; with visibility into health expenditure, fraud detection, supply chain efficiency, and whether health financing schemes are paying providers correctly and on time and reaching intended beneficiaries, providing the evidence base for informed resource allocation decisions.
- **Development partners and donors** benefit from infrastructure that outlasts individual funding cycles; with their investments building upon a shared foundation, rather than duplicating it.
- **Researchers** benefit from access to more complete and consistent health data — under appropriate consent and governance — supporting studies, evaluation, and evidence generation, which is more difficult to support when data is fragmented.
- **The commercial sector** can innovate on top of the shared infrastructure, building new value-added services and applications rather than recreating core components.
- **DPI Authorities** can leverage DPI-H to extend the utility of foundational DPI into contexts it was not designed to handle independently.
- **The health system as a whole** benefits from the compounding returns of interoperability and shared DPI, rather than degrading under the weight of fragmentation.

head.prose:
- **Patients** benefit in two distinct ways that should be kept analytically separate because they have different distributional effects: first, as a **reference point** — the axis around which clinical history, identity, and entitlements retain coherence as they follow the person across facilities and programmes rather than being reconstructed at each encounter, which requires no digital action from the individual and benefits everyone equally; and second, as an **active participant** accessing, managing, or contributing to their own records, which depends on individual activation and unequally distributed capabilities (including connectivity, device access, language fluency, health literacy, and digital literacy) and must therefore be supported by assisted and non-digital pathways of equivalent standing so that benefits do not accrue disproportionately to more advantaged groups.
- **Health workers** benefit from reduced administrative burden, fewer duplicate data entry tasks, and access to more complete and reliable information at the point of care, provided workflows and training are matched to varying levels of digital literacy and local working conditions.
- **Health programme managers** gain a consistent, cross-cutting data foundation that supports monitoring, evaluation, and resource planning across programmes rather than within silos — and, as data is aggregated across programmes and sectors, a basis for the intelligence that informs sector objectives, financing decisions, and operational guidelines.

base.prose: DPI-H does not eliminate the need for programme-specific and point-of-service applications. It provides the foundation upon which they can be built more efficiently, connected more reliably, and sustained more affordably — making every subsequent investment in the health system more productive than it would otherwise be.

head.prose: DPI-H does not eliminate the need for programme-specific and point-of-service applications. It provides the foundation upon which they can be built more efficiently, connected more reliably, and sustained more affordably — making every subsequent investment in the health system more productive than it would otherwise be. Because capabilities that depend on individual digital activation tend to be exercised first by those with higher income, education, connectivity, and digital confidence, the primary value case for DPI-H should rest on the systemic capabilities and continuity it creates for every person as a reference point regardless of whether they personally use a digital channel, while pairing any self-service capability with assisted and non-digital routes of equivalent standing.

base.prose: The first goal is **building trusted data foundations**. The core principle is that health data should be "*captured once and used many times*”. Countries currently invest heavily in reporting systems where the same data is re-entered at multiple levels of the system, leading to high burden, low quality, and limited comparability. The architecture defines the shared infrastructure that enables a single, high-quality data capture to support clinical care, facility management, population analytics including CRVS and mortality, public health monitoring, and domestic AI development simultaneously.

head.prose: The first goal is **building trusted data foundations**. The core principle is that health data should be "*captured once and used many times*”. Countries currently invest heavily in reporting systems where the same data is re-entered at multiple levels of the system, leading to high burden, low quality, and limited comparability. The architecture defines the shared infrastructure that enables a single, high-quality data capture — including across offline-first, assisted, and paper-bridged workflows and with explicit attention to populations missing from or underrepresented in formal datasets — to support clinical care, facility management, population analytics including CRVS and mortality, public health monitoring, and domestic AI development simultaneously.

base.prose: The fourth goal is **establishing** **trusted personal health records** with every person having a right to their own health record. The architecture supports individuals having access to secure, portable, and verifiable records of their health encounters, vaccinations, diagnoses, and treatments — records that follow them across providers and that they control through meaningful consent mechanisms.

head.prose: The fourth goal is **establishing** **trusted personal health records** with every person having a right to their own health record. The architecture supports individuals having access to secure, portable, and verifiable records of their health encounters, vaccinations, diagnoses, and treatments — records that follow them across providers and that they control through meaningful, accessible consent mechanisms, including assisted, delegated, and non-digital pathways of equivalent standing so that exercising rights over one's record never depends exclusively on individual smartphone ownership, fluency in an official language, or personal digital literacy.

base.prose: The outcomes these goals describe are not automatic. The extent to which they are realised depends on the quality of implementation and the context in which it takes place; evidence to date shows that benefits anticipated in design are not always borne out in practice. For this reason, the implementation of DPI-H should be evaluated as it proceeds — to evidence the benefits actually delivered, identify and mitigate risks, and share learning across programmes and countries. Together, these goals point towards a health system that has moved beyond digitisation as an end in itself — toward a system that is more equitable in who it reaches, more efficient in how it operates, more responsive to the people who deliver care, and more resilient in the face of the challenges that are increasingly certain to come.

head.prose: The outcomes these goals describe are not automatic. In every country, a proportion of the population cannot or chooses not to use self-service digital channels, and routine internet or device use is distinct from both basic digital skills and the health literacy needed to find, understand, and appraise health information. If the architecture's goals were achievable only through personal digital channels, the goals themselves would encode exclusion; accordingly, every function on which a person's access to care, rights, or health entitlements depends should maintain a non-digital or assisted route of equivalent standing as an operational readiness condition for deployment rather than a future aspiration. The extent to which these goals are realised depends on the quality of implementation and the context in which it takes place; evidence to date shows that benefits anticipated in design are not always borne out in practice. For this reason, the implementation of DPI-H should be evaluated as it proceeds — to evidence the benefits actually delivered, assess distributional effects across populations experiencing overlapping disadvantages, identify and mitigate exclusion risks, and share learning across programmes and countries. base.prose: Countries should design their DPI-H architecture to serve all populations equitably, including those in remote, under-resourced, or marginalised settings. At the level of the architecture, this is a structural concern and it shapes how the architecture as a whole is arranged so that the populations and settings least well served are not designed out of it.

head.prose: Countries should design their DPI-H architecture to serve all populations equitably, including those in remote, rural, mountainous, under-resourced, or marginalised settings. At the level of the architecture, equity and inclusion are structural concerns that encompass not only geographic, connectivity, and institutional constraints, but also user-side capability, socioeconomic, and sociocultural realities across the life course: variation in functional ability and disability (including changes in vision, hearing, dexterity, and cognition across age groups, as recognised in accessibility standards such as ITU-T F.780.2), language, general and health literacy, digital literacy and confidence among both patients and health workers, gender, affordability, cultural acceptability, and protection against discriminatory data practices. Unless these factors are treated as architectural concerns rather than interface afterthoughts, a service may be technically available yet practically unusable, and the populations and settings least well served risk being designed out of the system.

base.prose:
- The architecture should scale to context — designed so that the capability required to participate matches the resources of different settings, allowing it to be implemented and operated where infrastructure, connectivity, and institutional capacity are limited, not only where they are abundant.
- It should degrade gracefully rather than exclude. The absence of a given foundational layer — continuous connectivity, a mature national identity system, particular infrastructure — should reduce what is available rather than lock a setting or a population out entirely, so that participation does not depend on prerequisites that the least-served cannot meet.

• The architecture should scale to context — designed so that the capability required to participate matches the resources of different settings, allowing it to be implemented and operated where infrastructure, connectivity, and institutional capacity are limited, not only where they are abundant.
  • It should degrade gracefully rather than exclude. The absence of a given foundational layer — continuous connectivity, a mature national identity system, particular infrastructure — should reduce what is available rather than lock a setting or a population out entirely, so that participation does not depend on prerequisites that the least-served cannot meet.

head.prose:
- **Scale to context and support offline-first operation.** The architecture should be designed so that the capability required to participate matches the resources of different settings — including rural, remote, and mountainous areas with intermittent connectivity — through offline-first workflows, local caching, asynchronous synchronisation, and low-bandwidth exchange patterns, as well as low-complexity workflows suited to varying levels of digital literacy among health workers and administrative staff.
- **Degrade gracefully and guarantee non-digital routes of equivalent standing.** The absence of a given foundational layer — continuous connectivity, a mature national identity system, personal digital devices, or particular facility infrastructure — should reduce what is automated rather than lock a setting or population out entirely. Every function on which a right, clinical service, or health entitlement depends must maintain an assisted and non-digital route of equivalent standing (such as paper-bridged, facility-mediated, or community-health-worker-assisted pathways) so that participation, care access, and consent never depend on individual smartphone ownership or any single digital channel.
- **Accommodate variation in functional ability, disability, and literacy across the life course.** Countries should require age-inclusive and disability-accessible interaction patterns aligned with international accessibility standards (such as WCAG and ITU-T F.780.2), multimodal channels (including visual, audio, voice, USSD, and tactile formats), plain-language communication, and accessible consent mechanisms — including assisted, delegated, or documented oral consent where legally permitted rather than relying solely on written forms or self-service digital interfaces.
- **Treat language as a clinical data-quality and semantic requirement, not only a presentation concern.** The architecture must not assume that the person seeking care and the health worker share a fluent language — an assumption that routinely fails in multilingual states, rural communities served by clinicians trained in a national or administrative language, and migrant, refugee, or displacement settings. History or consent captured across an unbridged language barrier is systematically less complete and less accurate, and that deficit propagates directly into shared registries and longitudinal records. Supporting local languages, culturally acceptable communication, interpreter or mediation workflows, and the capability to capture history in the person's own language and render it accurately into the working language and governed terminology of the health system should therefore be treated as a data-quality and conformance requirement for systems that write to the shared record.
- **Assess distributional effects, ensure affordability, and guard against discriminatory data practices.** Major architectural, standards, and deployment decisions should be evaluated for their distributional effects — examining who gains access, who bears data-entry and compliance burdens, and who risks exclusion — supported by affordable access channels, representative usability testing across diverse population groups and health workers, disaggregated monitoring for differential outcomes and overlapping disadvantages, and safeguards against discriminatory profiling or unnecessary collection of sensitive data.

head.prose: The architecture's responsibility is to be structured so that serving the least-served — across geography, connectivity, functional ability, language, literacy, and socioeconomic circumstance — is built into core specifications, workflows, and conformance expectations as a coherent property of the system rather than treated as an exception.

base.prose:
- **Subsidiarity.** Decision authority should sit at the lowest level at which it can be exercised effectively. Operational decisions should not require strategic deliberation, and strategic decisions should not be delegated to operational bodies.
- **Separation of mandate and execution.** Strategic governance sets direction, defines scope boundaries and safeguards the long-term viability of the infrastructure; operational governance executes within those boundaries and has defined pathways to escalate when matters fall outside them.
- **Inclusive representation.** Governance structures should actively represent the communities most dependent on the infrastructure and least able to advocate for themselves through conventional political or market processes — including rural populations, women, displaced persons, and those served by under-resourced health systems. Representation of this kind should be more than advisory; governance design should give the interests of these communities genuine weight in strategic decisions, not nominal inclusion only. Translating nominal representation into real influence is a persistent challenge, and the mechanisms for pursuing it are set out in 3.4.3.
- **Financial sustainability as a governance mandate.** Digital health experience shows that technically promising systems often fail to sustain or scale when they remain dependent on short-term project funding, underestimated operating costs, weak institutional ownership, or insufficient integration into routine health system operations. \cite{lefevre-2021-road-to-nowhere,huang-2017-beyond-pilotitis,labrique-2018-best-practices-scaling} Governance should therefore treat the financial continuity of shared infrastructure not as a downstream implementation concern but as a core strategic mandate, with defined accountability, monitoring and response mechanisms.
- **Prevention of resource overuse.** Shared digital infrastructure should be governed so that no single programme, institution, vendor, or user group can place disproportionate demand on shared capacity, support resources, or operating budgets in ways that reduce service quality for others. Governance should establish usage policies, contribution expectations, monitoring, and enforcement mechanisms proportionate to the scale and diversity of its users. \cite{hardin-1968-tragedy-commons,ostrom-1990-governing-commons}
- **Transparency and accountability.** Governance decisions — including resource allocation, prioritisation and enforcement — should be documented, disclosed to the appropriate stakeholders, and open to review. Accountability without transparency is not accountability.
- **Adaptability and learning.** Governance structures should evolve as the infrastructure matures, as the ecosystem of actors changes, and as new risks and opportunities emerge. Static governance in a dynamic environment produces fragility. The purpose of this adaptability is to remain responsive to needs on the ground and to manage change well, rather than to control or prevent it. Since many risks and constraints become apparent only once a system is in use, governance should include ongoing evaluation of systems in operation, surfacing unintended consequences and emerging governance challenges so they can be addressed. \cite{greenhalgh-2017-beyond-adoption}

- **Subsidiarity.** Decision authority should sit at the lowest level at which it can be exercised effectively. Operational decisions should not require strategic deliberation, and strategic decisions should not be delegated to operational bodies.
- **Separation of mandate and execution.** Strategic governance sets direction, defines scope boundaries and safeguards the long-term viability of the infrastructure; operational governance executes within those boundaries and has defined pathways to escalate when matters fall outside them.
- **Inclusive representation and intersectional equity.** Governance structures should actively represent the communities most dependent on the infrastructure and least able to advocate for themselves through conventional political or market processes — including rural and remote populations, women, persons with disabilities, older adults, linguistic minorities, migrants and displaced persons, and those served by under-resourced health systems. Because systems may appear equitable in aggregate while performing poorly for people experiencing overlapping disadvantages, and because vulnerable populations may be missing from formal datasets altogether, governance must address intersectional equity across representation, access, system performance, and health outcomes — distinguishing measurable health differences (*health inequalities*) from avoidable, unfair, and remediable disparities (*health inequities*). Representation of this kind should be more than advisory; governance design should give the interests and community-defined priorities of these groups genuine weight in strategic decisions and require explicit assessment of the distributional effects of major decisions, as set out in 3.4.3.
- **Financial sustainability as a governance mandate.** Digital health experience shows that technically promising systems often fail to sustain or scale when they remain dependent on short-term project funding, underestimated operating costs, weak institutional ownership, or insufficient integration into routine health system operations. \cite{lefevre-2021-road-to-nowhere,huang-2017-beyond-pilotitis,labrique-2018-best-practices-scaling} Governance should therefore treat the financial continuity of shared infrastructure not as a downstream implementation concern but as a core strategic mandate, with defined accountability, monitoring and response mechanisms.
- **Prevention of resource overuse.** Shared digital infrastructure should be governed so that no single programme, institution, vendor, or user group can place disproportionate demand on shared capacity, support resources, or operating budgets in ways that reduce service quality for others. Governance should establish usage policies, contribution expectations, monitoring, and enforcement mechanisms proportionate to the scale and diversity of its users. \cite{hardin-1968-tragedy-commons,ostrom-1990-governing-commons}
- **Transparency and accountability.** Governance decisions — including resource allocation, prioritisation and enforcement — should be documented, disclosed to the appropriate stakeholders, and open to review. Accountability without transparency is not accountability.
- **Adaptability and learning.** Governance structures should evolve as the infrastructure matures, as the ecosystem of actors changes, and as new risks and opportunities emerge. Static governance in a dynamic environment produces fragility. The purpose of this adaptability is to remain responsive to needs on the ground and to manage change well, rather than to control or prevent it. Since many risks and constraints become apparent only once a system is in use, governance should include ongoing evaluation of systems in operation, surfacing unintended consequences and emerging governance challenges so they can be addressed. \cite{greenhalgh-2017-beyond-adoption}

base.prose: **Operationalising** **equity in governance bodies.** Design considerations include formal representation of civil society and community health advocates with a demonstrated constituency in underserved populations; geographic representation across subnational regions, particularly where health system capacity varies; gender and linguistic inclusion in the composition of governance bodies; mechanisms for soliciting and incorporating feedback from communities that lack organised representation; and explicit criteria by which equity impacts are assessed when major decisions are made.
base.html: Operationalising equity in governance bodies. Design considerations include formal representation of civil society and community health advocates with a demonstrated constituency in underserved populations; geographic representation across subnational regions, particularly where health system capacity varies; gender and linguistic inclusion in the composition of governance bodies; mechanisms for soliciting and incorporating feedback from communities that lack organised representation; and explicit criteria by which equity impacts are assessed when major decisions are made.

head.prose: **Operationalising** **equity and distributional impact assessment in governance.** Representation within governance bodies is necessary but not sufficient; governance must also assess and act on the actual distributional effects of architectural, standards, and policy decisions. Design considerations include: formal representation of civil society, disability and patient organisations, and community health advocates with a demonstrated constituency in underserved populations; geographic representation across subnational regions, particularly where health system capacity and connectivity vary; gender, disability, and linguistic inclusion in the composition of governance bodies; mechanisms for soliciting and incorporating feedback and community-defined priorities from populations that lack organised representation; and mandatory **equity-impact assessments** for major architectural, procurement, and governance decisions. Such assessments should examine who gains access and under what preconditions, who bears data-entry, administrative, and compliance burdens (across frontline health workers, under-resourced facilities, and patients), who risks exclusion when digital channels or identity requirements are introduced, whether assisted and non-digital routes of equivalent standing are maintained, and whether benefits and risks are distributed fairly across regions and population groups. Where lawful, proportionate, and ethically justified, governance should require evaluation across combinations of overlapping characteristics and contexts — such as poverty, disability, functional ability, language, literacy, geography, migration status, age, gender, and digital exclusion — rather than relying solely on single-group averages, while requiring explicit attention to populations missing from formal datasets, missing contextual meaning (including where patient and clinician do not share a fluent language), and cultural and linguistic fit without unnecessary collection of sensitive personal data.

base.prose: A reference architecture describes what a system needs to do and how it should behave — but for countries to translate architectural intent into implemented systems, they need a more concrete layer of specification: profiles that define the data structures, roles, transaction patterns, and integration interfaces that give the architecture its practical form. This section addresses that need, providing guidance on the minimum level of specification that countries should establish regardless of the technology choices they make in implementation.

head.prose: A reference architecture describes what a system needs to do and how it should behave — but for countries to translate architectural intent into implemented systems, they need a more concrete layer of specification: profiles that define the data structures, roles, transaction patterns, and integration interfaces that give the architecture its practical form. This section addresses that need, providing guidance on the minimum level of specification that countries should establish regardless of the technology choices they make in implementation. To ensure that the equity and inclusion principle (Section 2.3) is carried consistently into practice rather than left as an aspiration, countries should embed a dedicated **inclusion and accessibility workstream** across readiness assessment, profiling, procurement, conformance testing, rollout, impact measurement, workforce capacity building, and financing — operationalising accessibility across functional abilities, multilingual and cross-language clinical capture, offline-first and low-bandwidth operation, support for varying health worker and patient digital literacy, assisted access, and non-digital routes of equivalent standing at every stage of implementation.

base.prose: For the core registries, minimum data models should address at least the following: for the client registry, the minimum demographic and identity attributes required to uniquely identify a person across health system interactions; for the facility registry, the minimum attributes required to describe a health service delivery point, including its location, service capabilities, and operational status; for the health workforce registry, the minimum attributes required to describe a licensed health worker, including their credentials, specialisation, and deployment; and for the product registry, the minimum attributes required to describe a regulated health product, including its identity, classification, and regulatory status. For terminology services and the logical information model repository, minimum profiles should address the metadata requirements for versioning, validity periods, and content integrity described in the semantic governance infrastructure section.

head.prose: For the core registries, minimum data models should address at least the following: for the client registry, the minimum demographic and identity attributes required to uniquely identify a person across health system interactions — supporting alternative and assisted identification pathways where a foundational national identifier is absent, and capturing preferred language and communication or accessibility support needs without requiring unnecessary sensitive data that could expose vulnerable populations; for the facility registry, the minimum attributes required to describe a health service delivery point, including its location, service capabilities, accessibility features, connectivity profile, and operational status; for the health workforce registry, the minimum attributes required to describe a licensed or authorised health worker, including their credentials, specialisation, language capabilities, and deployment; and for the product registry, the minimum attributes required to describe a regulated health product, including its identity, classification, and regulatory status. For terminology services and the logical information model repository, minimum profiles should address the metadata requirements for versioning, validity periods, multilingual designations and cross-language mappings (so that history captured in a patient's language is faithfully represented in the working language and coded terminology of the health system), provenance for assisted or paper-bridged data capture, and content integrity described in the semantic governance infrastructure section.

WHO SMART Guidelines offer a worked example of this practice.[^39] The operational layer — the digital adaptation kit — defines a set of generic personas: depersonalised, context-free descriptions of the human and system actors involved in delivering a health service, set out alongside the data elements, workflows, and decision logic for a given domain. In the corresponding implementation guide, these personas are expressed as computable actor definitions against which workflows, capability statements, and access rules are anchored. The same discipline applies to shared infrastructure. For each DPI-H component, countries should define the minimum set of actors and roles that participate in its transactions — for a registry, for example, the registrant, the verifying authority, and the consuming system — and govern these role schemas through the same mechanisms used for data models and terminology. Defining actors explicitly, and reusing a common set across components, keeps access control, attribution, and workflow consistent across the ecosystem rather than re-invented for each system.

[^39]: WHO SMART Guidelines (Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable). The digital adaptation kit (L2) defines generic personas among its standardised components, which are represented as computable actor definitions in the corresponding FHIR implementation guide (L3). \cite{who-smart-guidelines-lancet-2021}

head.prose:
WHO SMART Guidelines offer a worked example of this practice.[^39] The operational layer — the digital adaptation kit — defines a set of generic personas: depersonalised, context-free descriptions of the human and system actors involved in delivering a health service, set out alongside the data elements, workflows, and decision logic for a given domain. The same discipline applies to shared infrastructure. For each DPI-H component, countries should define the minimum set of actors and roles that participate in its transactions — for a registry, for example, the registrant, the verifying authority, and the consuming system — and govern these role schemas through the same mechanisms used for data models and terminology. Actor and workflow specifications should explicitly include assisted-access, delegated-consent, interpreter or linguistic-mediation, and paper-to-digital bridging roles (such as community health workers, facility clerks, or authorised caregivers acting with a person), rather than assuming that patients interact solely through personal devices or share a fluent language with the clinician. Defining actors explicitly, and reusing a common set across components, keeps access control, attribution, and workflow consistent across the ecosystem rather than re-invented for each system.

The modular structure this logical decoupling enables allows countries to adopt capabilities incrementally, without redesigning the entire ecosystem. The physical implementation can then be centralised, distributed, or hybrid:

Across all physical topologies, implementation profiles for rural, remote, mountainous, or infrastructure-constrained areas should specify **offline-first workflows, local data caching, asynchronous store-and-forward synchronisation, and low-bandwidth exchange patterns** so that limited or intermittent internet connectivity never interrupts clinical care or excludes peripheral facilities and outreach teams from the shared architecture. base.prose: Profiles and specifications are useful only if compliance with them can be verified. Countries should establish minimum conformance requirements for each DPI-H component and define the testing mechanisms through which conformance is assessed. An interoperability test bed \cite{ec-interoperability-test-bed} — an openly available, standards-based testing environment offering validators, simulators, and test-management tooling — supports FHIR conformance testing and can be adapted to country-specific implementation profiles, giving countries a shared means of verification rather than one rebuilt from scratch for each procurement. Countries should consider requiring conformance certification against published profiles as a condition of approval for procurement of DPI-H components, so that every system entering the national digital health ecosystem contributes to interoperability rather than undermining it.

As part of the inclusion and accessibility workstream, procurement requirements, conformance testing, and pre-rollout readiness assessments should also verify accessibility across functional abilities (aligned with standards such as WCAG and ITU-T F.780.2), multilingual and cross-language data capture, offline-first and low-bandwidth operation, representative usability testing with health workers of varying digital literacy and with underserved patient groups, and the operational readiness of assisted and non-digital routes of equivalent standing for every function on which care access, rights, or health entitlements depend. Countries should consider requiring both technical and inclusion conformance certification against published profiles as a condition of procurement approval and deployment go/no-go decisions for DPI-H components, so that every system entering the national digital health ecosystem advances both interoperability and equitable access.

- **Component coverage** — which REDDHI components are in place, at what level of functionality, and with what geographic and population reach (the realisation-based coverage measure of section 3.7, applied over time).
- **Standards conformance** — the extent to which deployed components and existing systems conform to open standards, expose standard APIs, and use governed terminology and data models.

- **Enterprise and solution architects,** who maintain the national architecture and translate it into specific solution designs.
- **Information and FHIR modellers,** who design the data models, FHIR profiles, and actor definitions that make the architecture implementable, and keep them aligned with the reference profiles.
- **Terminology and semantic specialists,** who curate value sets, code systems, and mappings (for example to SNOMED CT/GPS, ICD-11, and LOINC) and operate the semantic governance processes.
- **Standards and interoperability specialists,** who specify exchange patterns, integration interfaces, and conformance tests.
- **Security and privacy architects,** who design the protection, consent, and access-control mechanisms that shared health data depends on.
- **Integration and implementation engineers,** who build and connect components and migrate data from legacy systems.
- **Data governance and stewardship roles,** who oversee data quality, access, and accountability.
- **Clinical and public-health informaticians,** who keep the architecture grounded in the realities of care delivery and programme need.
- **Change and programme managers,** who carry the organisational and workflow changes that new infrastructure requires.

- **Enterprise and solution architects,** who maintain the national architecture and translate it into specific solution designs.
- **Information and FHIR modellers,** who design the data models, FHIR profiles, and actor definitions that make the architecture implementable, and keep them aligned with the reference profiles.
- **Terminology and semantic specialists,** who curate value sets, code systems, and mappings (for example to SNOMED CT/GPS, ICD-11, and LOINC), including multilingual designations and cross-language clinical mappings, and operate the semantic governance processes.
- **Standards and interoperability specialists,** who specify exchange patterns, offline-first and low-bandwidth integration interfaces, and conformance tests.
- **Security and privacy architects,** who design the protection, consent, and access-control mechanisms that shared health data depends on.
- **Integration and implementation engineers,** who build and connect components and migrate data from legacy systems.
- **Data governance and stewardship roles,** who oversee data quality, access, equity-impact monitoring, and accountability.
- **Clinical and public-health informaticians,** who keep the architecture grounded in the realities of care delivery and programme need.
- **Accessibility, inclusion, and user-research specialists,** who ensure that interfaces, workflows, and assisted or non-digital service pathways accommodate variation in functional ability, disability, language, health literacy, and digital literacy among both patients and health workers.
- **Change and programme managers,** who carry the organisational, training, and workflow changes that new infrastructure requires.

base.prose: Capacity is not only technical. Introducing shared infrastructure changes how programmes work, how data is shared, and where decisions are made, and these changes are sustained only where the accompanying change management — stakeholder engagement, training, workflow redesign, and clear communication of benefit — is planned and resourced as deliberately as the technology itself.

head.prose: Capacity is not only technical or limited to specialist architecture teams. Introducing shared infrastructure changes how programmes work, how data is captured and shared, and where decisions are made, and these changes are sustained only where the accompanying change management — stakeholder engagement, structured training, workflow redesign, and clear communication of benefit — is planned and resourced as deliberately as the technology itself. In particular, countries should address two widespread implementation barriers explicitly: first, **variability in digital literacy among healthcare professionals and administrative staff** (which affects adoption and data quality in high-, middle-, and low-income settings alike) by defining minimum digital health competencies for frontline roles and providing structured pre-service and in-service training, protected learning time, mentoring, and low-complexity point-of-care workflows; and second, **general illiteracy, low health literacy, and limited digital literacy among patients, alongside linguistic diversity and cultural factors affecting acceptability and trust**, by resourcing multilingual patient navigation, community health worker and interpreter mediation, culturally adapted communication, and assisted and non-digital service pathways of equivalent standing.

base.prose: Whatever the mix, the value case has to be evidenced. The benefits case set out in the roadmap (section 4.1) and the progress measures in section 4.4 — coverage, standards conformance, governance maturity, and outcome linkage — provide the basis for showing Ministries of Finance and partners what shared infrastructure is delivering in return for its recurrent cost, and for sustaining the case for continued investment.

head.prose: Whatever the mix, financing plans should explicitly budget for the **inclusion and accessibility workstream** across the lifecycle of the architecture — including offline-first and low-bandwidth connectivity for rural and mountainous facilities, accessibility compliance and representative testing, multilingual and cross-language support, structured digital-competency training for health workers, patient navigation, and the sustained operation of assisted and non-digital routes of equivalent standing — so that cost savings are never achieved by shifting administrative burdens or exclusion onto underserved populations or frontline staff. The value case also has to be evidenced: the benefits case set out in the roadmap (section 4.1) and the progress and distributional equity measures in section 4.4 — coverage, standards conformance, governance maturity, and outcome linkage — provide the basis for showing Ministries of Finance and partners what shared infrastructure is delivering in return for its recurrent cost, and for sustaining the case for continued investment.

base.prose: It is also relevant that not all emerging technologies draw on data held in the shared infrastructure. Some consumer-facing applications operate independently of health-system data, using information entered by individuals or collected through personal devices to offer self-management support or lifestyle advice, and these can deliver value without accessing shared records or interoperating with wider health information systems. The architecture described here concerns those technologies that depend on, or contribute to, the shared health data foundation, and it is for these that the relationship set out below is decisive.

head.prose: It is also relevant that not all emerging technologies draw on data held in the shared infrastructure. Some consumer-facing applications operate independently of health-system data, using information entered by individuals or collected through personal devices to offer self-management support or lifestyle advice, and these can deliver value without accessing shared records or interoperating with wider health information systems. However, because their benefits depend on **individual activation**, personal device ownership, reliable and affordable connectivity, fluency in supported languages, functional ability, general and digital literacy, and often a stable digital identity, reliance on standalone consumer-facing tools can exclude underserved populations and widen health inequities. Where health systems endorse, integrate, or rely on patient-facing digital tools, countries should assess the risk of digital exclusion and require accessibility across functional abilities, affordability, multilingual and cross-language support (without assuming the person and health worker share a language), support for varying patient and health worker digital literacy, and **assisted and non-digital pathways of equivalent standing** for any function on which care access, rights, or entitlements depend. The architecture described in this chapter concerns those technologies that depend on, or contribute to, the shared health data foundation — where value accrues to every person as a reference point regardless of personal device ownership — and it is for these that the relationship set out below is decisive.

base.prose: Equity and safety warrant particular attention. A model trained on data that is poorly governed or unrepresentative of the population it serves can reproduce and magnify existing inequities, and because it does so consistently and at scale, the effect can be harder to notice than an individual error. Attention to the representativeness and quality of the underlying data is therefore not a separate ethical exercise but part of the same data-foundation discipline on which performance depends.

head.prose: Equity and safety warrant particular attention. A model trained on data that is poorly governed or unrepresentative of the population it serves can reproduce and magnify existing inequities, and because it does so consistently and at scale, the effect can be harder to notice than an individual error. Moreover, systems that appear equitable in aggregate or across single demographic categories may still perform poorly for people experiencing overlapping disadvantages — across combinations of poverty, disability, functional ability, language, literacy, geography, migration status, age, gender, and digital exclusion — or fail populations that are missing from formal datasets altogether or whose clinical history was captured across a language barrier without adequate contextual meaning. Where lawful, proportionate, and ethically justified, countries should require intersectional validation and ongoing distributional monitoring of AI-enabled tools, account for missing populations and cultural and linguistic fit without unnecessary collection of sensitive data, distinguish measurable health differences from avoidable and unjust health inequities, and preserve human clinical oversight and assisted or non-digital fallback pathways. Attention to the representativeness, contextual fidelity, and quality of the underlying data is therefore not a separate ethical exercise but part of the same data-foundation discipline on which clinical safety and performance depend.
